newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Visa sees U.S. probe end around April.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Visa sees U.S. probe end around April.

text.p: A U.S. Department of Justice probe of the competitiveness of the U.S. credit card market is not likely to be over before April, Paul Allen, executive vice president and general counsel of the VISA U.S.A. card association, said Friday in an interview.
At the same time, Allen expressed confidence that the probe would end with no charges being filed against Visa.
The probe has focused on a Visa bylaw which bars Visa members in the U.S. from issuing cards of American Express Co and Dean Witter Discover & Co.

"I suspect that the (antitrust) division will come to some closure with respect to this matter probably by the end of April," Allen said. He acknowledged that there have been published reports about a "showdown" meeting next week but he said that there was "no particular significance" to any meeting next week and that meetings have been taking place in person or on the telephone virtually weekly.

Asked if he saw any room for the parties to come to an agreement, Allen responded, "I don't see it happening." He said he believes Visa is correct on the facts and the law and sees no reason to back down.

"As a matter of antitrust law, as a matter of competition policy, this just doesn't make sense," Allen said, referring to American Express's arguments that the Visa bylaw is unfair. "They want to get the government to carry their baggage, and we say 'no,'" he said.

Allen asserted that American Express card products are more expensive than bank cards for merchants, and also more expensive for consumers. He said it would be a strange use of antitrust policy to help a company that provides a more expensive product compete in the marketplace.

Allen said a private antitrust suit recently filed in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of New York by Wal-Mart Stores Inc and others is totally unrelated, and Visa also believes it will prevail in that matter.

Allen said the plaintiffs are in essence seeking a lower price for processing debit cards by challenging Visa arrangements as illegal "tying" of products. Allen said the Wal-Mart suit is at a very preliminary stage.
American Express has argued that it believes certain U.S. banks are interested in doing business with American Express but their hands are tied by the Visa bylaw.
